{{distinguish|Family of sets}}
{{no footnotes|date=October 2025}}
{{Short description|Collection of objects, associated with an index set}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''family''', or '''indexed family''', is a collection of [[Mathematical object|objects]], each associated with an element, known as an '''index''', that belongs to some [[index set]].

For example, a family of [[real number]]s, indexed by the set of [[integer]]s, is a collection of real numbers, where a given function selects one real number for each integer (possibly the same) as indexing.

More formally, an indexed family is a [[Function (mathematics)|mathematical function]] together with its [[Domain of a function|domain]] <math>I</math> and [[Image (mathematics)|image]] <math>X</math> (that is, indexed families and mathematical functions are technically identical, just points of view are different). Often the [[Element (mathematics)|elements]] of the set <math>X</math> are referred to as making up the family. In this view, an indexed family is interpreted as a collection of indexed elements, instead of a function. The set <math>I</math> is called the ''index set'' of the family, and <math>X</math> is the ''indexed set''.

[[Sequence|Sequences]] are one type of families indexed by [[Natural number|natural numbers]]. In general, the index set <math>I</math> is not restricted to be [[Countable set|countable]]. For example, one could consider an uncountable family of subsets of the natural numbers indexed by the real numbers.

==Definition==
Let <math>I</math> and <math>X</math> be sets. A '''family of elements of <math>X</math> indexed by <math>I</math>''', denoted <math>(x_i)_{i\in I}</math>, is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f:I\to X</math> such that
<!-- not sure and I don't have time to research for this but a family is an application and a function is an application. So a family should be explained as an application and not a function --><math display="block">
 f(i)= x_i
</math>
for all <math>i \in I</math>.<ref>{{Mathworld |title=Family |id=Family |access-date=14 January 2026}}</ref> The element <math>x_i</math> is known as the term of index <math>i</math>.
Notation using different brackets, such as <math>\{x_i\}_{i\in I}</math> is also valid.

[[Function (mathematics)|Functions]] and indexed families are formally equivalent, since any function <math>f</math> with a [[Domain of a function|domain]] <math>I</math> induces a family <math>(f(i))_{i \in I}</math> and conversely. (The terms "mapping" for functions and "indexing" for indexed families are equivalent.) Being an element of a family is equivalent to being in the range of the corresponding function. In practice, however, a family is viewed as a collection, rather than a function. 

Any set <math>X</math> gives rise to a family <math>\left(x_t\right)_{t \in X},</math> where <math>X</math> is indexed by itself (meaning that <math>f</math> is the identity function). However, families differ from sets in that the same object can appear multiple times with different indices in a family, whereas a set is a collection of distinct objects. A family contains any element exactly once [[if and only if]] the corresponding function is [[injective]].

An indexed family <math>\left(x_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> defines a set <math>\mathcal{X} = \{x_i : i \in I\},</math> that is, the image of <math>I</math> under <math>f.</math> Since the mapping <math>f</math> is not required to be [[Injective function|injective]], there may exist <math>i, j \in I</math> with <math>i \neq j</math> such that <math>x_i = x_j.</math> Thus, <math>| \mathcal{X}| \leq |I|</math>, where <math>|A|</math> denotes the [[cardinality]] of the set <math>A.</math> For example, the sequence <math>\left( (-1)^i \right)_{i\in \N} </math> indexed by the natural numbers <math>\N = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}</math> has image set <math>\left\{(-1)^i : i \in \N\right\} = \{-1,1\}.</math> In addition, the set <math>\{ x_i : i \in I \}</math> does not carry information about any structures on <math>I.</math> Hence, by using a set instead of the family, some information might be lost. For example, an ordering on the index set of a family induces an ordering on the family, but no ordering on the corresponding image set. 

===Indexed subfamily===

An indexed family <math>\left(B_i\right)_{i \in J}</math> is a '''subfamily''' of an indexed family <math>\left(A_i\right)_{i \in I},</math> [[if and only if]] <math>J</math> is a subset of <math>I</math> and <math>B_i = A_i</math> holds for all <math>i \in J.</math>

==Examples==

===Indexed vectors===

For example, consider the following sentence:
{{Quote
|text=The vectors <math>v_1, \ldots, v_n</math> are [[linearly independent]].
}}
Here <math>\left(v_i\right)_{i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}}</math> denotes a family of vectors. The <math>i</math>-th vector <math>v_i</math> only makes sense with respect to this family, as sets are unordered so there is no <math>i</math>-th vector of a set. Furthermore, [[linear independence]] is defined as a property of a collection; it therefore is important if those vectors are linearly independent as a set or as a family. For example, if we consider <math>n = 2</math> and <math>v_1 = v_2 = (1, 0)</math> as the same vector, then the ''set'' of them consists of only one element (as a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] is a collection of unordered distinct elements) and is linearly independent, but the family contains the same element twice (since indexed differently) and is linearly dependent (same vectors are linearly dependent).

===Matrices===

Suppose a text states the following:
{{Quote
|text=A square matrix <math>A</math> is invertible, [[if and only if]] the rows of <math>A</math> are linearly independent.
}}
As in the previous example, it is important that the rows of <math>A</math> are linearly independent as a family, not as a set. For example, consider the matrix
<math display=block>A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.</math>
The ''set'' of the rows consists of a single element <math>(1, 1)</math> as a set is made of unique elements so it is linearly independent, but the matrix is not invertible as the matrix [[determinant]] is 0. On the other hand, the ''family'' of the rows contains two elements indexed differently such as the 1st row <math>(1, 1)</math> and the 2nd row <math>(1, 1)</math> so it is linearly dependent. The statement is therefore correct if it refers to the family of rows, but wrong if it refers to the set of rows. (The statement is also correct when "the rows" is interpreted as referring to a [[multiset]], in which the elements are also kept distinct but which lacks some of the structure of an indexed family.)

===Other examples===

Let <math>\mathbf{n}</math> be the finite set <math>\{1, 2, \ldots n\},</math> where <math>n</math> is a positive [[integer]].
* An [[ordered pair]] (2-[[tuple]]) is a family indexed by the set of two elements, <math>\mathbf{2} = \{1, 2\};</math> each element of the ordered pair is indexed by an element of the set <math>\mathbf{2}.</math>
* An [[tuple|<math>n</math>-tuple]] is a family indexed by the set <math>\mathbf{n}.</math>
* An infinite [[sequence]] is a family indexed by the [[natural numbers]].
* A [[Tuple|list]] is an <math>n</math>-tuple for an unspecified <math>n,</math> or an infinite sequence.
* An <math>n \times m</math> [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] is a family indexed by the [[Cartesian product]] <math>\mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{m}</math> which elements are ordered pairs; for example, <math>(2, 5)</math> indexing the matrix element at the 2nd row and the 5th column.
* A [[Net (mathematics)|net]] is a family indexed by a [[directed set]].

==Operations on indexed families==

Index sets are often used in sums and other similar operations. For example, if <math>\left(a_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is an indexed family of numbers, the sum of all those numbers is denoted by
<math display=block>\sum_{i \in I} a_i.</math>

When <math>\left(A_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is a [[family of sets]], the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of all those sets is denoted by
<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i.</math>

Likewise for [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]]s and [[Cartesian product]]s.

==Usage in category theory==
{{main|Diagram (category theory)}}

The analogous concept in [[category theory]] is called a '''[[Diagram (category theory)|diagram]]'''. A diagram is a [[functor]] giving rise to an indexed family of objects in a [[Category theory|category]] {{math|'''''C'''''}}, indexed by another category {{math|'''''J'''''}}, and related by [[morphism]]s depending on two indices.
